questions.stem: Employment relation primarily refers to the relationship between

options.A: employer and employee

questions.explanation: Employment relation is fundamentally the legal and social relationship that exists between an employer and an employee arising from a contract of employment.

questions.stem: The employment relationship is best described as a nexus of

options.A: rights and obligations

questions.explanation: The employment relationship creates a nexus of mutual rights and obligations for both parties - the employer and the employee.

questions.stem: Which term is used interchangeably with 'employment relation' in most academic literature?

options.A: industrial relation

questions.explanation: Employment relation and industrial relation are used interchangeably in most academic and policy literature to describe the study of the work relationship.

questions.stem: The legal basis of the employment relationship is typically established through a

options.A: contract of employment

questions.explanation: A contract of employment, whether written or implied, forms the legal foundation of the employment relationship.

questions.stem: Employment relations is primarily concerned with regulating

options.A: the world of work

questions.explanation: Employment relations as a field focuses on regulating and understanding all aspects of the world of work, including pay, conditions, and worker rights.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the essence of the employment relation?

options.A: exchange of labour for remuneration

questions.explanation: At its core, the employment relation involves a worker providing labour in exchange for wages or other forms of remuneration from the employer.

questions.stem: The concept of 'subordination' in employment relations refers to

options.A: employee's duty to follow employer's direction

questions.explanation: Subordination is a key element distinguishing employment from other work arrangements; it means the employee is subject to the employer's direction and control.

questions.stem: Which element distinguishes an employee from an independent contractor in employment relations?

options.A: control and direction by the employer

questions.explanation: The degree of control exercised by the employer over how, when, and where work is done is the primary distinguishing element between an employee and an independent contractor.

questions.stem: Employment relation acknowledges that there is an inherent __________ between employers and employees.

options.A: conflict of interest

questions.explanation: Employment relations theory recognises that employers and employees have an inherent conflict of interest over the distribution of profits, control of work, and working conditions.

questions.stem: The 'psychological contract' in employment relations refers to

options.A: unwritten expectations between employer and employee
options.B: a mental health agreement at work
options.C: a formal written contract signed by both parties

questions.explanation: The psychological contract comprises the unwritten, informal expectations and obligations that each party perceives in the employment relationship.

questions.stem: Industrial relations as a field of study was largely shaped by the rise of

options.A: factory-based capitalism

questions.explanation: The emergence of factory-based capitalism during the Industrial Revolution created the mass employment relationships that gave rise to industrial relations as a discipline.

questions.stem: Which approach views employment relations as a system of rules governing the workplace?

options.A: systems approach

questions.explanation: John Dunlop's systems approach views industrial relations as a sub-system of society that produces a web of rules governing the employment relationship.

questions.stem: The unitary perspective of employment relations assumes that the workplace is

options.A: a harmonious team with shared goals

questions.explanation: The unitary perspective views the organisation as one cohesive team sharing common goals, where conflict is seen as irrational or the work of troublemakers.

questions.stem: The pluralist perspective of employment relations recognises

options.A: multiple legitimate interest groups in the workplace
options.C: the state as the only regulator

questions.explanation: Pluralism acknowledges that employers, employees, and unions are distinct groups with legitimate but sometimes competing interests that must be balanced.

questions.stem: The Marxist/radical perspective of employment relations argues that conflict at work is

options.A: structural and inevitable under capitalism

questions.explanation: The Marxist perspective holds that conflict is a structural feature of capitalist employment relations, rooted in the exploitation of labour by capital.

questions.stem: Employment relations differs from human resource management primarily in its emphasis on

options.A: collective rather than individual relationships

questions.explanation: Employment relations focuses on collective bargaining, unions, and group interests, whereas HRM tends to emphasise individual employee management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a core subject of employment/industrial relations?

options.A: marketing strategy

questions.explanation: Marketing strategy is outside the scope of employment relations; the discipline focuses on collective bargaining, unionism, labour law, and workplace conflict resolution.

questions.stem: Industrial relations is described as a study of the 'rules of the game' at work. Who coined this idea?

options.A: John Dunlop

questions.explanation: John Dunlop's 1958 work 'Industrial Relations Systems' described employment relations as a system producing a web of rules - essentially the 'rules of the game' in the workplace.

questions.stem: Employment relations covers the relationship between workers and employers at which levels?

options.A: individual, organisational, and societal
options.B: local, national, and international trade only

questions.explanation: Employment relations operates at multiple levels: the individual employment contract, the organisational collective agreement, and the broader societal legal framework.

questions.stem: Which of the following outcomes is a direct product of employment relations processes?

options.A: collective agreements

questions.explanation: Collective agreements - negotiated between unions and employers - are a key institutional output of the employment relations process.

questions.stem: The multidisciplinary nature of employment relations means it draws knowledge from

options.A: several academic disciplines

questions.explanation: Employment relations is multidisciplinary because it borrows concepts, theories, and methods from economics, sociology, law, psychology, history, and political science.

questions.stem: Which discipline contributes the concept of 'labour market' to employment relations?

options.A: economics

questions.explanation: Economics contributes foundational concepts like the labour market, wage determination, supply and demand for labour, and efficiency theories to employment relations.

questions.stem: Sociology contributes which concept to the study of employment relations?

options.A: class conflict and power

questions.explanation: Sociology brings concepts of class structure, power dynamics, social stratification, and group behaviour to the analysis of employment relationships.

questions.stem: Psychology contributes to employment relations through its focus on

options.A: individual motivation and behaviour at work

questions.explanation: Psychology informs employment relations by explaining how motivation, attitudes, perception, and personality influence worker behaviour and the employment relationship.

questions.stem: The legal dimension of employment relations is concerned with

options.A: rights, duties, and enforcement in the workplace

questions.explanation: Labour law defines statutory rights and duties of employers and employees, sets minimum standards, and provides mechanisms for enforcement and dispute resolution.

questions.stem: Political science contributes to employment relations by analysing

options.A: the role of the state and power in regulating work

questions.explanation: Political science examines how government, state power, and policy decisions shape employment relations, including legislation, labour courts, and collective bargaining frameworks.

questions.stem: History contributes to employment relations by providing

options.A: context for how work relationships evolved over time

questions.explanation: Historical analysis helps understand how industrialisation, labour movements, and policy shifts shaped current employment relations structures and practices.

questions.stem: The multidisciplinary nature of employment relations is best justified because

options.A: work affects every dimension of human social life
options.B: it makes the subject harder to study

questions.explanation: Because work touches economic, social, legal, psychological, and political dimensions of human life, a single discipline cannot adequately explain employment relations.

questions.stem: Which academic discipline is most directly linked to the study of collective bargaining in employment relations?

options.A: political science and law

questions.explanation: Collective bargaining involves the exercise of power (political science) and the creation of enforceable agreements (law), making these the most directly relevant disciplines.

questions.stem: Management science contributes to employment relations by focusing on

options.A: organising and directing human resources efficiently

questions.explanation: Management science provides frameworks for organising, directing, motivating, and controlling employees within the employment relationship.

questions.stem: The formal study of industrial relations emerged primarily as a result of

options.A: the Industrial Revolution

questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution (18th-19th century) created large-scale factory employment, urban labour forces, and the employment conflicts that necessitated a systematic study of industrial relations.

questions.stem: Before industrialisation, the dominant economic system in Europe was

options.A: feudalism

questions.explanation: Feudalism was the dominant pre-industrial economic and social system in Europe, characterised by lords owning land and serfs providing labour in exchange for protection.

questions.stem: The transition from feudalism to capitalism is most associated with

options.A: enclosure of common lands and the rise of wage labour
options.B: the invention of the printing press

questions.explanation: The enclosure movement dispossessed peasants of common land, forcing them to sell their labour for wages - a fundamental shift enabling capitalist employment relations.

questions.stem: The first academic programme in industrial relations was established at

options.A: Cornell University

questions.explanation: Cornell University established one of the earliest formal industrial relations programmes in 1945, signalling the academic recognition of the discipline.

questions.stem: The early labour movement arose primarily in response to

options.A: poor working conditions and low wages in factories

questions.explanation: Workers organised collectively because industrial factories subjected them to harsh conditions, long hours, low pay, and dangerous environments with no legal protections.

questions.stem: The 'laissez-faire' approach in early industrial employment relations meant

options.A: minimal state intervention in the labour market

questions.explanation: Laissez-faire ideology held that market forces should freely determine wages and conditions, leaving workers without state protection and enabling employer exploitation.

questions.stem: Which event is widely regarded as a catalyst for early labour legislation in Britain?

options.A: Chartist movement and early union agitation

questions.explanation: The Chartist movement and union agitation in the 19th century pressured the British government to enact early labour laws improving working conditions.

questions.stem: The establishment of the International Labour Organization (ILO) in 1919 was significant to employment relations because it

options.A: set international labour standards and rights

questions.explanation: The ILO was created after World War I to promote social justice and internationally recognised human and labour rights, shaping employment relations worldwide.

questions.stem: Which school of thought, emerging from the late 19th century, advocated scientific management as a solution to labour problems?

options.A: Taylorism

questions.explanation: Frederick Winslow Taylor's scientific management (Taylorism) proposed that systematic work study and standardisation could improve efficiency and reduce labour conflicts.

questions.stem: The post-World War II period in employment relations is characterised by

options.A: the growth of collective bargaining and welfare states

questions.explanation: After WWII, most Western nations expanded collective bargaining rights and built welfare states, creating a 'golden age' of industrial relations with strong union influence.

questions.stem: The feudal system was characterised by which form of labour relationship?

options.A: lord and serf (unfree labour)

questions.explanation: In the feudal system, serfs were bound to the lord's land, providing labour services in exchange for protection - a form of unfree or coerced labour.

questions.stem: A key feature of the feudal economic system was the ownership of

options.A: land as the primary means of production

questions.explanation: In feudalism, land was the dominant means of production, and social power derived from land ownership, unlike capitalism where capital and machinery are central.

questions.stem: Which obligation did serfs owe to their lord in the feudal system?

options.A: labour services on the lord's land
options.C: military service to the king only

questions.explanation: Serfs were obligated to work a portion of their time on the lord's demesne (land) as a form of rent payment, a defining feature of feudal labour relations.

questions.stem: The factory system, which emerged during the Industrial Revolution, is best described as

options.A: centralised production using machinery and wage labour

questions.explanation: The factory system concentrated workers, machines, and raw materials in one location, using wage labour under managerial supervision - a radical departure from prior production methods.

questions.stem: Which factor was most responsible for the decline of the feudal system?

options.A: the Black Death reducing labour supply and increasing worker bargaining power

questions.explanation: The Black Death (1347-1351) killed a third of Europe's population, creating labour scarcity that gave peasants bargaining power and undermined feudal obligations.

questions.stem: The factory system introduced a new form of labour discipline primarily through

options.A: clock-based time management and supervision

questions.explanation: Factory work imposed strict clock-time discipline - set hours, shifts, and managerial supervision - replacing the task-based and seasonal rhythms of pre-industrial work.

questions.stem: Child and female labour in early factories was significant because it

options.A: highlighted the lack of protective employment legislation

questions.explanation: The widespread exploitation of children and women in early factories, working long hours in dangerous conditions, exposed the absence of employment protections and drove reform movements.

questions.stem: In the feudal system, disputes between lords and serfs were resolved primarily through

options.A: manorial courts controlled by the lord

questions.explanation: Feudal dispute resolution was administered through manorial courts presided over by the lord, giving lords enormous power over serfs with no independent arbitration.

questions.stem: The 'putting-out system' that preceded the factory system involved

options.A: merchants supplying raw materials to home-based workers

questions.explanation: In the putting-out (or domestic) system, merchants distributed raw materials to rural households who produced goods at home, bridging feudal cottage production and the factory system.

questions.stem: Which technological innovation most directly enabled the factory system?

options.A: the steam engine

questions.explanation: James Watt's steam engine provided the mechanised power source that made large-scale factory production possible, transforming employment relations fundamentally.

questions.stem: A primary objective of employment relations is to

options.A: maintain industrial peace and harmony

questions.explanation: Employment relations aims to establish mechanisms for managing conflict and promoting cooperative workplace relationships that sustain industrial peace.

questions.stem: Employment relations seeks to ensure that workers receive

options.A: fair wages and decent working conditions

questions.explanation: A core objective of employment relations is to protect workers from exploitation by establishing fair pay, reasonable hours, and safe working conditions.

questions.stem: Which objective of employment relations focuses on giving workers a voice in decisions that affect them?

options.A: worker participation and democracy

questions.explanation: Employment relations aims to democratise the workplace by ensuring workers have meaningful channels to participate in decisions affecting their work lives.

questions.stem: Employment relations legislation aims to protect employees from

options.A: unfair dismissal and discrimination

questions.explanation: A key legislative objective is to prevent employers from arbitrarily dismissing workers or discriminating against them on grounds such as race, gender, or religion.

questions.stem: The objective of 'efficiency' in employment relations refers to

options.A: productive use of human resources

questions.explanation: Efficiency as an objective of employment relations involves ensuring that human resources are utilised productively, benefiting both the employer and the broader economy.

questions.stem: Employment relations aims to achieve 'equity' which means

options.A: fair treatment of all parties in the employment relationship
options.D: equal number of male and female managers

questions.explanation: Equity in employment relations refers to just and impartial treatment of employers and employees, ensuring that neither party is exploited or unfairly disadvantaged.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an economic objective of employment relations?

options.A: promoting economic growth through stable labour markets
options.D: fixing prices of goods and services

questions.explanation: Stable employment relations reduce strikes and disruptions, creating predictable labour markets that support investment, productivity, and economic growth.

questions.stem: The social objective of employment relations is to

options.A: reduce inequality and promote social cohesion

questions.explanation: Employment relations has a social objective of reducing workplace-based inequality through fair pay, non-discrimination, and inclusive practices that strengthen social cohesion.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is central to achieving the objectives of employment relations?

options.A: collective bargaining

questions.explanation: Collective bargaining between unions and employers is the primary institutional mechanism through which employment relations objectives like fair wages and conditions are pursued.

questions.stem: Employment relations objectives also include promoting

options.A: occupational health and safety

questions.explanation: Protecting workers from hazards at work is a foundational objective of employment relations, achieved through legislation, collective agreements, and workplace practices.

questions.stem: The three main stakeholders in employment relations are

options.A: employers, employees/unions, and the state

questions.explanation: Employment relations theory identifies employers, employees (represented by trade unions), and the state as the three principal actors whose interactions shape workplace rules.

questions.stem: The role of employers in employment relations includes

options.A: providing employment and setting workplace policies

questions.explanation: Employers create jobs, determine pay and conditions within legal limits, and establish workplace policies - making them central actors in employment relations.

questions.stem: Employer associations perform which function in employment relations?

options.A: representing employers collectively in bargaining and lobbying

questions.explanation: Employer associations aggregate the interests of multiple employers to negotiate with unions collectively and lobby governments on labour policy.

questions.stem: The primary role of trade unions in employment relations is to

options.A: protect and advance workers' interests

questions.explanation: Trade unions exist to represent workers collectively, bargain for better wages and conditions, and protect members from arbitrary employer action.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of a trade union?

options.A: hiring and firing employees

questions.explanation: Hiring and firing are managerial prerogatives of the employer; unions do not engage in employment decisions but rather negotiate the terms under which such decisions are made.

questions.stem: The state's role in employment relations includes

options.A: enacting labour legislation and providing dispute resolution

questions.explanation: The state regulates employment relations through legislation (minimum wage, anti-discrimination laws) and provides institutions like labour courts for dispute resolution.

questions.stem: A 'shop steward' in employment relations is

options.A: a workplace-level trade union representative

questions.explanation: A shop steward is an elected trade union representative within a workplace who handles grievances, communicates union policy, and represents members in dealings with management.

questions.stem: The role of a labour court or industrial tribunal is to

options.A: adjudicate employment disputes between parties

questions.explanation: Labour courts and industrial tribunals serve a judicial function, hearing and deciding disputes about employment rights, unfair dismissal, discrimination, and breach of contract.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'managerial prerogative' in employment relations?

options.A: the employer's right to manage and direct the workforce
options.B: the union's right to veto all workplace decisions
options.C: the state's authority to nationalise industries
options.D: the employee's right to refuse all instructions

questions.explanation: Managerial prerogative refers to the employer's residual authority to make decisions about how the business is run, including directing employees - subject to legal and contractual limits.

questions.stem: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) influence employment relations by

options.A: advocating for labour rights and social standards

questions.explanation: NGOs such as human rights organisations pressure governments and corporations to uphold labour rights, particularly in global supply chains and for vulnerable worker groups.

questions.stem: Which economic factor most directly affects employment relations?

options.A: unemployment levels

questions.explanation: High unemployment weakens workers' bargaining power, while low unemployment strengthens it - making unemployment levels a key economic factor shaping employment relations.

questions.stem: Globalisation affects employment relations by

options.A: creating competitive pressure to reduce labour costs

questions.explanation: Globalisation exposes firms to international competition, pressuring them to reduce labour costs, which can undermine wages, conditions, and union strength.

questions.stem: Technological change affects employment relations primarily by

options.A: altering the nature and organisation of work
options.D: reducing the importance of labour law

questions.explanation: Technology changes the skills required, the tasks performed, and the organisation of work, reshaping employment relationships and creating new employment relations challenges.

questions.stem: Inflation affects employment relations because

options.A: it erodes real wages and triggers wage claims
options.C: it strengthens the currency and improves exports
options.D: it reduces the cost of production

questions.explanation: Rising inflation reduces workers' purchasing power (real wages), prompting unions to push for wage increases that match or exceed inflation - a common source of industrial disputes.

questions.stem: Which political factor most significantly affects employment relations?

options.A: the ideology and policies of the governing party

questions.explanation: Government ideology shapes labour legislation, union rights, minimum wage policy, and the extent of state intervention - all fundamentally affecting employment relations.

questions.stem: The decline in trade union membership in many countries since the 1980s is primarily attributed to

options.A: deindustrialisation and growth of the service sector

questions.explanation: The shift from manufacturing (traditionally highly unionised) to service industries (harder to organise) has been the primary structural cause of declining union density.

questions.stem: Which cultural factor influences employment relations in a society?

options.A: attitudes toward authority and collectivism

questions.explanation: Cultural attitudes - such as willingness to challenge authority, collectivist versus individualist orientations - shape how workers organise, how management relates to workers, and the character of employment relations.

questions.stem: The size of an organisation affects employment relations because

options.A: larger organisations typically have more formalised employment relations structures
options.B: small firms always have better employment relations
options.C: size has no relevance to employment relations
options.D: large firms are exempt from labour law

questions.explanation: Large organisations tend to have formal HR departments, written procedures, collective agreements, and union recognition, while small firms often rely on informal and personal relationships.

questions.stem: The structure of the labour market (e.g., internal vs. external) affects employment relations by determining

options.A: how workers are recruited, rewarded, and retained

questions.explanation: Labour market structure shapes whether organisations fill vacancies internally (internal labour markets) or from outside, influencing pay scales, career paths, and worker commitment.

questions.stem: Demographic changes (such as an ageing workforce) affect employment relations by

options.A: creating pressures to rethink retirement, pensions, and age discrimination policies
options.B: automatically increasing wages for all workers
options.C: reducing the need for collective bargaining
options.D: eliminating the need for occupational health policies

questions.explanation: An ageing population increases the proportion of older workers, pressing organisations and governments to revisit retirement ages, pension provisions, and age-related discrimination in employment.

questions.stem: The concept of 'industrial action' refers to

options.A: collective action by workers to press their demands

questions.explanation: Industrial action - including strikes, go-slows, and work-to-rule - is a collective form of worker pressure used to advance employment relations objectives.

questions.stem: The 'gig economy' poses a challenge to traditional employment relations because

options.A: workers lack standard employment contracts and protections
options.B: it eliminates all forms of work
options.C: gig workers earn more than regular employees
options.D: the state fully regulates all gig platforms

questions.explanation: Gig workers are typically classified as independent contractors, excluding them from employment protections such as minimum wage, sick pay, and unfair dismissal rights.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a 'substantive rule' in employment relations?

options.A: the level of wages agreed in a collective agreement
options.B: the procedure for raising a grievance
options.C: the election process for union officers
options.D: the procedure for calling a strike ballot

questions.explanation: Substantive rules determine the actual content of employment (pay, hours, benefits), as opposed to procedural rules that govern how decisions are made.

questions.stem: A 'procedural rule' in employment relations governs

options.A: the process for handling disputes and negotiations
options.B: the rate of pay for overtime work
options.C: the number of holidays workers receive

questions.explanation: Procedural rules set out the methods and steps for conducting collective bargaining, resolving grievances, and taking industrial action - how things are done rather than what is agreed.

questions.stem: The term 'collective bargaining' refers to

options.A: negotiation between employers and trade unions on behalf of workers
options.B: individual salary negotiations between an employee and manager
options.C: government setting of all wages by law

questions.explanation: Collective bargaining is the process by which trade unions negotiate with employers on wages, hours, and conditions on behalf of their members.

questions.stem: Which of the following characterises 'voluntarism' in employment relations?

options.A: parties regulate their own relationship without state imposition
options.B: the state sets all terms and conditions of employment
options.C: unions are legally compelled to bargain
options.D: employers must always accept union demands

questions.explanation: Voluntarism is a tradition (especially British) where employers and unions prefer to regulate their relationship through voluntary collective bargaining rather than state-imposed legal rules.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of individual employment rights?

options.A: protection against unfair dismissal
options.B: the right to call a general strike
options.C: the right to set minimum wages

questions.explanation: Individual employment rights are those held by each worker regardless of union membership, such as the right not to be unfairly dismissed, to receive minimum wage, or to take maternity leave.

questions.stem: The concept of 'floor of rights' in employment law refers to

options.A: minimum statutory protections that cannot be bargained away
options.B: the physical floor space allocated to workers
options.C: the maximum benefit employees can receive
options.D: the lowest profit level a firm must maintain

questions.explanation: The floor of rights establishes minimum legal standards (e.g., minimum wage, maximum hours) below which neither collective agreements nor individual contracts can fall.

questions.stem: A 'lockout' in employment relations is when

options.A: an employer prevents workers from entering the workplace during a dispute
options.B: workers refuse to leave the factory
options.C: the government shuts down an industry

questions.explanation: A lockout is the employer's counterpart to a strike: the employer withholds work from employees to exert pressure during an industrial dispute.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the concept of 'labour power' in employment relations?

options.A: the capacity of workers to perform labour, sold to employers for wages
options.B: the physical strength of individual workers
options.D: the legal power of trade unions

questions.explanation: Labour power, a concept drawn from Marx, refers to the worker's capacity for work - a commodity sold to the employer in exchange for wages, distinct from the actual labour performed.

questions.stem: The 'wage-effort bargain' in employment relations refers to

options.A: the implicit exchange of worker effort for employer remuneration
options.B: a legal contract defining overtime rates
options.C: the union's official wage claim document

questions.explanation: The wage-effort bargain describes the ongoing negotiation - explicit or implicit - about how much effort workers provide in exchange for the wages and benefits they receive.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a 'craft union'?

options.A: it organises workers based on a specific skilled trade
options.B: it represents all workers in one industry

questions.explanation: Craft unions (e.g., plumbers, electricians) organise workers who share a specific skill or trade, contrasted with industrial unions that represent all workers in a sector.

questions.stem: An 'industrial union' differs from a craft union in that it

options.A: represents all workers in an industry regardless of skill or occupation

questions.explanation: Industrial unions organise all workers within a particular industry (e.g., mining, transport) regardless of their specific job or skill level, giving them broader membership.

questions.stem: The 'closed shop' arrangement in employment relations means

options.A: workers must be union members as a condition of employment
options.B: the factory is closed during holidays
options.D: the firm restricts recruitment to family members

questions.explanation: A closed shop (now illegal in many countries) was an arrangement requiring all employees in a workplace to belong to a specified trade union as a prerequisite for employment.

questions.stem: The ILO's 'Decent Work' agenda covers which four pillars?

options.A: employment creation, rights at work, social protection, and social dialogue

questions.explanation: The ILO's Decent Work Agenda comprises: opportunities for productive employment, respect for fundamental labour rights, adequate social protection, and inclusion in social dialogue.

questions.stem: The concept of 'industrial democracy' in employment relations refers to

options.A: giving workers meaningful participation in workplace decision-making
options.D: allowing workers to set their own wages

questions.explanation: Industrial democracy encompasses mechanisms - such as works councils, joint consultation, and board-level representation - that give employees a voice in decisions affecting their work.

questions.stem: A grievance procedure in employment relations is used to

options.A: address workers' complaints about their employment

questions.explanation: A grievance procedure provides a structured process through which employees can formally raise and resolve complaints about their treatment or working conditions.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents a 'macro-level' factor affecting employment relations?

options.A: national economic policy and labour legislation
options.C: the layout of a specific factory floor
options.D: a single firm's sick leave policy

questions.explanation: Macro-level factors operate at the societal or national level - including government economic policy, labour law, and macroeconomic conditions - shaping the broad environment of employment relations.

questions.stem: The 'employment at will' doctrine, common in parts of the United States, means

options.A: either party can terminate employment without cause
options.B: workers must resign voluntarily to leave
options.C: employers must provide a reason for all dismissals

questions.explanation: Employment at will allows either the employer or employee to end the employment relationship at any time for any reason (with some exceptions), giving employers wide dismissal latitude.

questions.stem: The fundamental goal of employment relations as a discipline is to

options.A: achieve a balance between employer efficiency and worker wellbeing
options.B: maximise corporate profits at all costs
options.C: eliminate all forms of workplace conflict

questions.explanation: Employment relations seeks the ongoing balance between the employer's need for productive and efficient operations and the employee's need for fair treatment, decent wages, and dignified work.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary duty of an employer in an employment relationship?

options.A: providing safe working conditions

questions.explanation: Employers have a fundamental legal and moral duty to provide a safe working environment, protecting employees from hazards and occupational risks.

questions.stem: The employer's duty to pay agreed wages falls under the category of

options.A: contractual obligation

questions.explanation: Payment of wages as agreed in the contract of employment is a legally enforceable contractual obligation of the employer, not a discretionary act.

questions.stem: The duty of an employer to 'mutual trust and confidence' means the employer must

options.A: not act in a way that destroys the employment relationship
options.D: promote every employee after two years

questions.explanation: The implied duty of mutual trust and confidence requires employers to refrain from conduct that would fundamentally undermine the employment relationship without reasonable cause.

questions.stem: An employer's duty to provide a reference is best described as

options.A: a limited duty not to give a misleading reference
options.B: an absolute duty to give a glowing reference
options.C: a duty imposed by collective agreement only
options.D: a duty that does not exist in law

questions.explanation: While employers are generally not obliged to provide references, if they do, they owe a duty of care to ensure the reference is accurate and not misleading.

questions.stem: Which legislation primarily governs the employer's duty regarding occupational health and safety?

options.A: Factories Act and associated health and safety legislation

questions.explanation: Factories Acts and occupational health and safety statutes impose duties on employers to maintain safe premises, equipment, and systems of work.

questions.stem: The employer's duty to provide work (as opposed to merely paying wages) is most relevant to

options.A: skilled workers who need practice to maintain their skills

questions.explanation: Courts have recognised a duty to provide actual work for employees whose skills may atrophy without practice - such as surgeons, actors, or skilled tradespeople.

questions.stem: An employer who fails to provide a safe system of work may be liable under

options.A: the tort of negligence

questions.explanation: Employers owe employees a duty of care in negligence; failure to provide a safe system of work that results in injury exposes the employer to tortious liability.

questions.stem: The employer's duty of non-discrimination requires employers to

options.A: treat all employees fairly regardless of protected characteristics
options.B: pay identical wages to all workers
options.C: hire only workers from the local community
options.D: give preference to senior workers in all decisions

questions.explanation: Anti-discrimination legislation prohibits employers from treating employees less favourably on grounds such as race, gender, religion, disability, or age.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an employer's implied duty under common law?

options.A: to indemnify employees for expenses incurred in the course of employment
options.B: to pay all employees equal wages
options.D: to provide free transport to work

questions.explanation: An implied contractual duty exists at common law for employers to reimburse employees for reasonable expenses necessarily incurred while performing their employment duties.

questions.stem: The Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) dimension of employers' duties extends to

options.A: broader obligations to society and the environment beyond legal minimums
options.C: paying only the statutory minimum wage

questions.explanation: CSR reflects a view that employers' responsibilities extend beyond legal compliance to include ethical treatment of workers, community investment, and environmental sustainability.

questions.stem: An employee's primary obligation to the employer is to

options.A: render personal service as agreed in the contract
options.C: recruit new workers for the firm
options.D: represent the employer in government meetings

questions.explanation: The fundamental obligation of an employee is to personally perform the duties agreed in the contract of employment - employment is a personal contract.

questions.stem: The employee's duty of fidelity or loyalty requires the employee to

options.A: act in the employer's best interest and not work against the employer
options.B: disclose the employer's trade secrets to competitors
options.D: report to work seven days a week

questions.explanation: The duty of fidelity obliges employees not to engage in activities that damage the employer's interests, such as working for competitors or misusing confidential information.

questions.stem: Which employee duty relates to not disclosing sensitive company information to third parties?

options.A: duty of confidentiality

questions.explanation: The duty of confidentiality (implied in all contracts of employment) prohibits employees from disclosing the employer's trade secrets or confidential business information.

questions.stem: Employees have a duty to obey lawful and reasonable instructions from their employer. This duty is limited by

options.A: instructions that are illegal or put the employee at serious risk
options.B: the number of years of service
options.D: the size of the employer's business

questions.explanation: Employees must follow reasonable lawful instructions, but they are not obliged to obey instructions that are unlawful, unethical, or that place them in serious physical danger.

questions.stem: The employee's right to receive wages is a

options.A: contractual and statutory right
options.B: voluntary benefit granted by the employer
options.D: right available only to unionised workers

questions.explanation: The right to receive agreed wages is both a contractual right (arising from the employment contract) and a statutory right (protected by minimum wage legislation).

questions.stem: The right to form and join trade unions is classified as a

options.A: fundamental labour right

questions.explanation: Freedom of association - including the right to form and join trade unions - is recognised as a fundamental labour right by the ILO and most national labour laws.

questions.stem: An employee's duty to exercise reasonable care and skill means

options.A: performing work to a competent standard
options.B: completing work as fast as possible regardless of quality
options.C: doing only tasks listed in the job description
options.D: working without supervision at all times

questions.explanation: Employees impliedly undertake to perform their duties with the level of competence and care that a reasonable person in that role would exercise.

questions.stem: The employee's right to a safe workplace is enforceable against the employer through

options.A: health and safety legislation and civil claims
options.C: voluntary employer codes of conduct only

questions.explanation: Employees can enforce their right to a safe workplace through health and safety regulatory bodies, employment tribunals, and civil negligence claims.

questions.stem: An employee's obligation of 'account' requires them to

options.A: account for any property or money belonging to the employer

questions.explanation: The duty to account obliges employees to keep proper records of and surrender to the employer any money, property, or benefits received in the course of employment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a statutory employee right in most jurisdictions?

options.A: the right to a company car
options.C: the right to paid annual leave
options.D: the right not to be unfairly dismissed

questions.explanation: A company car is a contractual benefit, not a statutory right; minimum wage, paid leave, and unfair dismissal protection are rights created by employment legislation.

questions.stem: Management prerogative refers to

options.A: the inherent right of management to direct and control the enterprise
options.B: the union's right to approve all management decisions
options.C: the government's power to nationalise firms
options.D: shareholders' rights to change the board of directors

questions.explanation: Management prerogative is the residual authority employers claim to make business decisions - including who to hire, how to organise work, and how to deploy resources - without requiring union consent.

questions.stem: Trade unions challenge management prerogative primarily through

options.A: collective bargaining and negotiating over workplace rules

questions.explanation: Unions restrict and shape management prerogative by negotiating collectively to establish agreed rules on wages, discipline, redundancy, and other workplace matters.

questions.stem: Which of the following decisions is typically considered a core area of management prerogative?

options.A: decisions about investment, production methods, and business strategy
options.B: the level of union subscription fees
options.D: the content of government labour policy

questions.explanation: Strategic business decisions - such as investment, technology adoption, and market strategy - are traditionally regarded as within the exclusive domain of managerial authority.

questions.stem: The concept of 'residual rights' in management prerogative means

options.A: management retains all rights not expressly given up in collective agreements
options.B: unions retain all rights not mentioned in law
options.C: workers own residual profits of the firm
options.D: governments retain rights over private firms

questions.explanation: The residual rights theory holds that management's authority is whatever remains after the specific rights bargained away to unions in collective agreements.

questions.stem: Union recognition by an employer is significant because it

options.A: obliges the employer to negotiate with the union on agreed matters
options.B: transfers ownership of the firm to the union
options.C: eliminates the employer's right to discipline workers
options.D: makes all management decisions subject to union veto

questions.explanation: Once a union is recognised, the employer is obligated to engage in collective bargaining with it on the scope of issues covered by that recognition.

questions.stem: The 'right to manage' doctrine is most associated with which perspective on employment relations?

options.A: the unitary perspective

questions.explanation: The unitary perspective stresses the employer's inherent right to manage the organisation as a cohesive unit, viewing union challenges to management as illegitimate interference.

questions.stem: Anti-union tactics by management aimed at preventing union formation are known as

options.A: union avoidance strategies

questions.explanation: Union avoidance strategies include tactics such as substitution (providing benefits to reduce union appeal) and suppression (actively discouraging or blocking unionisation).

questions.stem: When management makes a unilateral change to employment conditions without union consultation, this is called

options.A: unilateral action

questions.explanation: Unilateral action occurs when management imposes changes to terms and conditions without negotiating with the union - often a source of industrial disputes.

questions.stem: Which scenario represents a restriction on management prerogative by a trade union?

options.A: a collective agreement requiring redundancies to follow a 'last in, first out' rule
options.B: management deciding to expand the factory

questions.explanation: A collectively agreed redundancy procedure constrains management's freedom to choose whom to make redundant, demonstrating how unions limit management prerogative.

questions.stem: The expansion of collective bargaining into areas like pension schemes, staffing levels, and training represents

options.A: a broadening of union influence over management decisions

questions.explanation: As unions successfully negotiate over more subject areas beyond basic wages, they progressively narrow the scope of exclusive management prerogative.

questions.stem: Employee participation in employment relations refers to

options.A: workers having a say in decisions that affect their work
options.B: employees owning shares in all companies
options.C: workers setting the company's strategic direction alone

questions.explanation: Employee participation encompasses arrangements that give workers influence over workplace decisions, ranging from information sharing to co-determination.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a DIRECT form of employee participation?

options.A: team briefings and quality circles

questions.explanation: Direct participation involves employees themselves (not their representatives) engaging with management - examples include team briefings, suggestion schemes, and quality circles.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an INDIRECT form of employee participation?

options.A: works councils and union representation

questions.explanation: Indirect participation operates through elected or appointed representatives (union officials, works councillors) who act on behalf of employees in dealings with management.

questions.stem: A 'works council' is best described as

options.A: a joint body of employee representatives and management that discusses workplace issues
options.B: a court that hears workers' compensation cases
options.C: a committee that manages the employer's pension fund
options.D: a government agency overseeing factory safety

questions.explanation: Works councils are statutory or voluntary bodies in which elected employee representatives and management meet regularly to discuss issues such as working conditions, restructuring, and training.

questions.stem: Employee involvement (EI) differs from employee participation (EP) primarily in that

options.A: EI is management-initiated to align employees with company goals, while EP gives workers independent influence
options.B: EI is illegal while EP is compulsory
options.C: EI is collective while EP is individual
options.D: EI involves unions while EP excludes them

questions.explanation: Employee involvement is driven by management to secure commitment and productivity, whereas employee participation is about workers exercising independent influence over decisions affecting them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of financial participation by employees?

options.A: profit-sharing and employee share ownership
options.D: serving on a health and safety committee

questions.explanation: Financial participation gives employees a stake in the financial performance of the enterprise through mechanisms like profit-related pay, share ownership, and employee stock options.

questions.stem: The main argument FOR employee participation is that it

options.A: improves decision quality and increases worker commitment
options.C: eliminates the need for trade unions

questions.explanation: Advocates argue that participation harnesses workers' knowledge to improve decisions, raises morale, reduces absenteeism, and increases commitment to organisational goals.

questions.stem: The European Works Councils (EWC) Directive requires large multinational companies to

options.A: establish cross-border information and consultation bodies for employees
options.B: share all profits equally among European workers
options.C: allow unions to manage company operations
options.D: set identical wages across all European countries

questions.explanation: The EWC Directive mandates that qualifying multinationals operating in the EU create works councils that inform and consult employee representatives on transnational issues.

questions.stem: Worker representation on company boards of directors is known as

options.A: board-level employee representation or co-determination

questions.explanation: Co-determination (as practised in Germany) and board-level employee representation give workers direct influence over strategic corporate decisions at the highest governance level.

questions.stem: A suggestion scheme at the workplace is an example of which type of employee involvement?

options.A: upward problem-solving communication

questions.explanation: Suggestion schemes invite individual employees to submit ideas to management, representing upward communication and direct individual involvement in workplace improvement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an essential element for a valid contract of employment?

options.A: offer, acceptance, and consideration
options.B: a written document signed by both parties

questions.explanation: Like any contract, a contract of employment requires an offer (by the employer), acceptance (by the employee), and consideration (wages in exchange for labour) to be legally valid.

questions.stem: Express terms in an employment contract are

options.A: terms explicitly agreed and stated by the parties
options.B: terms automatically read in by law
options.C: terms negotiated by the trade union only
options.D: terms set by the government without negotiation

questions.explanation: Express terms are those that the parties have explicitly agreed upon, whether verbally or in writing - such as salary, job title, and working hours.

questions.stem: Implied terms in an employment contract are

options.A: terms not explicitly stated but incorporated by law, custom, or necessity
options.C: terms imposed by the trade union
options.D: terms that override all express terms

questions.explanation: Implied terms fill gaps in express agreements; they arise from statute (e.g., the duty of mutual trust), custom and practice, or necessity (e.g., the duty to obey lawful instructions).

questions.stem: The consideration provided by the employee in an employment contract is

options.A: the provision of their labour and service
options.B: the payment of a signing bonus

questions.explanation: In contract law, consideration must flow from both parties; the employee's consideration is their personal service (labour), while the employer's consideration is wages.

questions.stem: A 'written statement of particulars' of employment is

options.A: a statutory document setting out key employment terms

questions.explanation: Most employment statutes require employers to provide employees with a written statement of the main terms and conditions of their employment within a set period of starting work.

questions.stem: Which of the following is typically an express term in an employment contract?

options.A: the rate of pay and working hours
options.B: the duty of mutual trust and confidence
options.C: the duty to obey lawful instructions
options.D: the right to a safe workplace

questions.explanation: Pay and hours are the most fundamental express terms agreed between parties, whereas mutual trust, obedience, and safety are implied terms arising from law or common law.

questions.stem: A collective agreement incorporated into an individual employment contract becomes

options.A: legally binding on the individual employee

questions.explanation: When terms of a collective agreement (e.g., pay scales) are incorporated into individual employment contracts, they become enforceable contractual terms between the individual employer and employee.

questions.stem: The principle of 'privity of contract' in employment law means

options.A: only the parties to the contract can enforce its terms
options.B: the contract must be kept secret
options.C: the government must approve the contract
options.D: all employees in a firm share the same contract

questions.explanation: Privity of contract is the common law principle that only those who are parties to a contract - employer and employee - can sue to enforce its terms.

questions.stem: A 'restrictive covenant' in an employment contract is designed to

options.A: limit the employee's activities after leaving employment
options.B: increase the employee's wages after resignation
options.D: prevent the employer from relocating the business

questions.explanation: Restrictive covenants (post-termination restrictions) protect the employer's legitimate business interests by limiting an ex-employee's ability to compete, poach clients, or solicit former colleagues.

questions.stem: The employment contract is described as a 'personal contract' because

options.A: the employee cannot delegate their duties to another person
options.B: it must be signed in person at a government office
options.C: it can only be discussed with family members
options.D: it applies only to personal services outside work

questions.explanation: The personal nature of the employment contract means the employee must personally perform their duties; unlike commercial contracts, they cannot subcontract their labour to someone else.

questions.stem: In employment relations, conflict is defined as

options.A: incompatibility of goals or interests between parties in the employment relationship
options.B: the legal process of terminating employment
options.C: the management practice of setting performance targets
options.D: any communication between employer and employee

questions.explanation: Conflict in employment relations arises when the goals, interests, or values of employers and employees diverge - over pay, working conditions, control, or security.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of OVERT conflict in the workplace?

options.A: a formal strike by workers

questions.explanation: Overt conflict is open and visible - including strikes, go-slows, and other forms of industrial action - as opposed to covert forms like absenteeism or sabotage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of COVERT conflict in the workplace?

options.A: deliberate absenteeism and go-slow
options.D: a court-ordered injunction against industrial action

questions.explanation: Covert conflict involves hidden or indirect forms of worker resistance - such as deliberate absenteeism, poor quality work, or go-slows - that are less visible than formal industrial action.

questions.stem: Conflict at the INDIVIDUAL level in employment relations is typically expressed through

options.A: individual grievances and resignation

questions.explanation: Individual conflict is expressed through personal grievance procedures, disciplinary proceedings, and ultimately resignation - as opposed to collective action by groups of workers.

questions.stem: The view that conflict in the workplace is INEVITABLE is associated with which perspective?

options.A: pluralist and Marxist perspectives

questions.explanation: Both pluralism (multiple interest groups with competing claims) and Marxism (structural class conflict) regard workplace conflict as an inevitable feature of employment relations.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of conflict in employment relations?

options.A: shared goals between management and workers

questions.explanation: When management and workers share common goals, this reduces conflict; conflict arises from divergent interests - such as disputes over wages, conditions, and management decisions.

questions.stem: The term 'industrial dispute' in employment relations refers to

options.A: a collective disagreement between employers and workers or their unions
options.B: a lawsuit between two competing companies
options.C: a disagreement between the government and a private firm
options.D: an individual employee's resignation from a job

questions.explanation: An industrial dispute is a collective conflict between an employer (or employers' association) and workers (or their union) over terms and conditions of employment.

questions.stem: Functional conflict in employment relations is best described as

options.A: conflict that leads to constructive outcomes and improvements
options.C: conflict that destroys the employment relationship
options.D: conflict that is illegal under labour law

questions.explanation: Functional (constructive) conflict can stimulate innovation, surface important issues, and lead to improved practices - as opposed to dysfunctional conflict that harms organisational performance.

questions.stem: The distinction between 'rights disputes' and 'interest disputes' in employment relations is that

options.A: rights disputes concern existing entitlements while interest disputes concern new terms to be negotiated
options.B: rights disputes are individual while interest disputes are always collective
options.C: interest disputes involve legal rights while rights disputes involve economic claims
options.D: there is no meaningful distinction between the two

questions.explanation: Rights disputes arise over the interpretation or application of existing agreements or law, while interest disputes involve disagreements over what new terms should be agreed in future.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms is used to RESOLVE conflict in employment relations?

options.A: conciliation, mediation, and arbitration
options.C: share offers and bonus payments only

questions.explanation: Conflict resolution mechanisms in employment relations include conciliation (third party facilitates negotiation), mediation (third party proposes a solution), and arbitration (third party decides the outcome).

questions.stem: The unitary theory of conflict views industrial conflict as

options.A: irrational and caused by poor communication or troublemakers
options.B: a natural and inevitable feature of capitalist employment
options.C: a legitimate tool of worker empowerment

questions.explanation: Unitarists see the organisation as a harmonious team; when conflict occurs, they attribute it to misunderstandings, poor management, or the interference of agitators - not structural causes.

questions.stem: The pluralist theory of conflict views conflict as

options.A: natural, inevitable, and manageable through negotiation
options.C: proof of communist influence in the workplace

questions.explanation: Pluralists accept that multiple groups with different interests coexist in organisations; conflict is expected and can be managed constructively through collective bargaining and agreed procedures.

questions.stem: The Marxist (radical) theory of conflict argues that industrial conflict is ultimately rooted in

options.A: the exploitation of workers under capitalism
options.C: cultural differences between managers and workers

questions.explanation: Marxists argue that conflict is inherent in capitalist employment because owners of capital extract surplus value from workers' labour, creating an irreconcilable class antagonism.

questions.stem: The human relations theory of conflict, associated with Elton Mayo, suggests conflict is caused by

options.A: poor social relations and failure to meet workers' social needs

questions.explanation: The human relations school (Hawthorne studies) argued that conflict stems from managers ignoring workers' social and psychological needs, and that addressing these reduces conflict.

questions.stem: Systems theory (Dunlop) explains conflict as arising from

options.A: failure of the industrial relations system to produce adequate rules
options.B: individual personality clashes between managers and workers

questions.explanation: Dunlop's systems theory views conflict as a symptom of inadequate rule-making within the industrial relations system; where proper rules exist and are accepted, stability prevails.

questions.stem: Which theory of conflict advocates for the complete transformation of the capitalist system as the only solution?

options.A: Marxist/radical theory

questions.explanation: Marxists argue that because conflict is rooted in the class structure of capitalism, it cannot be truly resolved through collective bargaining or better management - only systemic change can eliminate it.

questions.stem: According to the pluralist theory, the most appropriate response to conflict is

options.A: collective bargaining and agreed dispute resolution procedures

questions.explanation: Pluralists see collective bargaining and institutional conflict resolution mechanisms as the appropriate means to manage the competing interests of employers, employees, and unions.

questions.stem: The unitarist solution to workplace conflict typically involves

options.A: improving communication, stronger management, and direct employee involvement
options.B: granting more power to trade unions
options.C: introducing compulsory arbitration by the state

questions.explanation: Since unitarists see conflict as irrational or caused by poor management, they favour direct communication, strong leadership, and employee involvement to build unity and prevent conflict.

questions.stem: The 'interactionist' perspective on conflict in organisations suggests that

options.A: some level of conflict is beneficial and should be encouraged
options.B: all conflict must be eliminated immediately

questions.explanation: The interactionist (or managerialist) view holds that a minimum level of conflict is functional and necessary to stimulate creativity, prevent stagnation, and drive organisational change.

questions.stem: Which of the following conflict theories is most closely aligned with a conservative, pro-management view?

options.A: unitary theory

questions.explanation: The unitary theory is most aligned with a pro-management view because it asserts that management's authority is legitimate, conflict is disruptive, and unions are unnecessary obstacles.

questions.stem: Collective bargaining is defined as

options.A: negotiation between employers and workers' representatives over employment terms
options.B: individual salary negotiations between an employee and a manager
options.C: the government setting wages for all workers by law

questions.explanation: Collective bargaining is the process by which trade unions negotiate with employers collectively on behalf of workers to determine wages, hours, and working conditions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a SUBSTANTIVE outcome of collective bargaining?

options.A: an agreed wage rate or working hours
options.B: a procedure for conducting future negotiations
options.C: the rules for calling a strike ballot

questions.explanation: Substantive outcomes of collective bargaining are the actual terms agreed - pay rates, hours, leave entitlements - as opposed to procedural outcomes that govern how future bargaining is conducted.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a PROCEDURAL outcome of collective bargaining?

options.A: an agreed grievance handling procedure
options.B: a pay increase for all workers

questions.explanation: Procedural outcomes of collective bargaining establish the rules and processes governing the employment relationship - such as dispute resolution, negotiation procedures, and union rights.

questions.stem: Enterprise-level bargaining takes place

options.A: between a single employer and a union at the firm level
options.B: across an entire industry or sector
options.D: at the international level between governments

questions.explanation: Enterprise or company-level bargaining occurs between a specific employer and the union(s) representing workers in that organisation - producing agreements specific to that workplace.

questions.stem: Industry-wide or sectoral collective bargaining is characterised by

options.A: negotiations covering all (or most) employers and workers in a sector
options.B: bargaining between one firm and one worker
options.C: the government setting wages for one company

questions.explanation: Sectoral or industry-wide bargaining involves employers' associations and trade unions negotiating agreements that apply to all enterprises within an industry, providing uniform minimum standards.

questions.stem: The concept of 'good faith bargaining' requires parties to

options.A: negotiate seriously and openly with the genuine intention of reaching agreement
options.B: always agree to all union demands
options.C: give the union access to all company financial data
options.D: accept compulsory arbitration if negotiations fail

questions.explanation: Good faith bargaining obliges both parties to engage sincerely in negotiations, provide relevant information, and genuinely attempt to reach a mutually acceptable agreement.

questions.stem: A 'closed shop' provision historically meant that collective bargaining covered

options.A: only union members who were compulsorily employed at the workplace
options.C: workers in a single department only

questions.explanation: In a closed shop arrangement, union membership was a condition of employment, meaning collective agreements covered a workforce that was 100% unionised.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'integrative bargaining'?

options.A: a win-win approach where both parties seek to expand the total gains

questions.explanation: Integrative (or interest-based) bargaining seeks solutions that satisfy the interests of both parties - expanding the 'pie' rather than competing over a fixed amount.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'distributive bargaining'?

options.A: a competitive process where one party's gain is the other's loss
options.B: a cooperative process to find shared solutions

questions.explanation: Distributive (or positional) bargaining treats negotiation as a zero-sum game - when one party wins a higher wage, the employer 'loses' that amount - producing adversarial negotiations.

questions.stem: The role of conciliation in collective bargaining disputes is to

options.A: assist the parties to reach their own voluntary agreement with a third party's help
options.B: impose a binding decision on the parties
options.D: prosecute the party causing the dispute

questions.explanation: Conciliation involves a neutral third party facilitating communication and negotiation between the disputing parties to help them reach a voluntary agreement - without imposing an outcome.

questions.stem: Arbitration in employment relations differs from conciliation in that arbitration

options.A: involves a third party making a binding or advisory decision
options.B: leaves the outcome entirely to the parties
options.C: requires union members to vote on any settlement

questions.explanation: In arbitration, a neutral arbitrator hears the submissions of both parties and issues a decision (award) which may be binding on both parties - unlike conciliation where the parties decide.

questions.stem: The scope of collective bargaining refers to

options.A: the range of subjects covered in negotiations
options.B: the number of workers in the union
options.C: the duration of the collective agreement
options.D: the level at which bargaining takes place

questions.explanation: Scope of bargaining refers to what is negotiated - whether it covers only wages and hours or extends to wider issues like job security, training, staffing levels, and pension arrangements.

questions.stem: A collective agreement is described as the 'industrial equivalent of legislation' because

options.A: it creates binding rules governing the employment relationship
options.D: it applies to all workers in the country

questions.explanation: Like legislation, a collective agreement creates enforceable rules - on pay, conditions, and procedures - that govern the employment relationship for the workers it covers.

questions.stem: Which factor has most contributed to the decline in collective bargaining coverage in many countries since the 1980s?

options.A: deindustrialisation, weakening of unions, and government deregulation

questions.explanation: The shift away from manufacturing, anti-union legislation, and neoliberal deregulation reduced union density and collective bargaining coverage across many developed economies from the 1980s onwards.

questions.stem: The 'bargaining unit' in collective bargaining refers to

options.A: the group of employees covered by a particular collective agreement
options.B: the committee of managers conducting negotiations
options.C: the government ministry overseeing the negotiations
options.D: the arbitration panel hearing a dispute

questions.explanation: The bargaining unit defines which employees are represented by the union in negotiations and to whom the resulting collective agreement applies.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'pattern bargaining'?

options.A: when agreements in one firm or sector are used as a template for others
options.B: when management imposes the same wage on all workers
options.C: when the government sets a uniform wage for all industries

questions.explanation: Pattern bargaining occurs when negotiated settlements in key agreements (e.g., a flagship company) set the standard that other employers and unions in the same sector follow.

questions.stem: The ILO Convention No. 98 specifically protects

options.A: the right to organise and collective bargaining
options.C: the right to a minimum wage

questions.explanation: ILO Convention No. 98 (1949) is a fundamental instrument protecting workers' rights to organise and engage in collective bargaining, prohibiting employer interference with union activities.

questions.stem: In collective bargaining, 'deadlock' occurs when

options.A: negotiations reach an impasse and neither party will move from their position
options.B: the union wins all its demands

questions.explanation: A deadlock (or impasse) arises when collective bargaining stalls because neither party is willing to make further concessions - often leading to industrial action or third-party intervention.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of collective bargaining?

options.A: providing criminal sanctions against employers
options.D: regulating the relationship between management and unions

questions.explanation: Criminal sanctions are a matter for the state and criminal law; collective bargaining is a private process between employers and unions focused on employment terms and workplace governance.

questions.stem: The concept of 'union density' is important in collective bargaining because

options.A: higher union membership gives unions greater bargaining power
options.B: it determines the size of the employer's profits
options.C: it sets the level of the minimum wage
options.D: it determines the number of government labour inspectors

questions.explanation: Union density (the proportion of workers who are union members) is a key determinant of union bargaining power; higher density means more workers can participate in collective action.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions would constitute a breach of the employee's duty of fidelity?

options.A: working for a direct competitor in secret while employed
options.B: joining a trade union without telling the employer
options.D: raising a formal grievance about working conditions

questions.explanation: Secretly working for a competitor while employed is a clear violation of the duty of fidelity/loyalty, as it places the employee's interests in direct conflict with those of the employer.

questions.stem: An employer who imposes a pay cut without employee consent may be liable for

options.A: breach of contract and constructive dismissal

questions.explanation: Unilaterally reducing wages breaches the express contractual term on pay; if the employee resigns in response to such a fundamental breach, they may claim constructive dismissal.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the link between management prerogative and collective bargaining?

options.A: unions narrow management prerogative by negotiating rules on previously unregulated decisions
options.B: management prerogative expands as union membership grows
options.C: collective bargaining eliminates all management authority
options.D: management prerogative and collective bargaining are completely unrelated

questions.explanation: Each time unions successfully negotiate agreed rules on a new subject area (e.g., job security, technology introduction), they restrict the space of unilateral management decision-making.

questions.stem: A quality circle is an example of employee participation that primarily aims to

options.A: improve production quality through worker input on workplace problems
options.B: give workers control over strategic investment decisions
options.C: replace management with elected worker committees

questions.explanation: Quality circles bring small groups of workers together voluntarily to identify, analyse, and solve quality and production problems - combining employee involvement with operational improvement.

questions.stem: The implied term of 'mutual trust and confidence' can be breached by an employer who

options.A: bullies or humiliates an employee without reasonable cause
options.B: insists on the employee following health and safety procedures
options.C: requires the employee to work their contracted hours
options.D: restructures the organisation after proper consultation

questions.explanation: Courts have found that bullying, humiliating, or seriously undermining an employee without justification destroys the relationship of trust and confidence, amounting to a breach of this implied term.

questions.stem: Which approach to resolving collective conflict requires BOTH parties to accept the outcome determined by a neutral third party?

options.A: binding arbitration

questions.explanation: In binding arbitration, both parties agree in advance to accept the arbitrator's award as final and binding - removing the need for further negotiation or industrial action.

questions.stem: A collective agreement that covers wages, hours, and disciplinary procedures is best described as

options.A: a comprehensive substantive and procedural agreement

questions.explanation: An agreement covering both the content of employment (wages, hours) and the processes for managing the relationship (disciplinary procedures) combines substantive and procedural elements.

questions.stem: The Marxist view of collective bargaining is that it

options.A: merely manages but does not resolve the underlying class conflict
options.B: fully eliminates exploitation in capitalist firms
options.C: gives workers complete control over production
options.D: is unnecessary in a free market economy

questions.explanation: Marxists accept that collective bargaining can improve workers' conditions at the margins, but argue it leaves the fundamental exploitative structure of capitalism intact.

questions.stem: Which of the following employment contract elements specifically addresses what happens at the END of the employment relationship?

options.A: notice period and termination clauses

questions.explanation: Notice period and termination clauses govern how the employment relationship is ended - setting out the minimum notice required and the grounds on which either party may terminate.

questions.stem: In employment relations, the concept of 'voice' refers to

options.A: employees' ability to express views and influence decisions in the workplace
options.C: the employer's right to issue instructions
options.D: the government's power to set labour standards

questions.explanation: Employee voice encompasses all the mechanisms - individual or collective - through which workers communicate their interests, concerns, and ideas and exert influence in the employment relationship.
